notes:
Here are verse-by-verse notes on **1 Corinthians 8**, drawn from the sources accessed.

---

## Overview

The chapter addresses meat sacrificed to idols — a pressing question in Corinth where nearly all public and much private meat had passed through pagan temples. Paul’s larger subject is the right use of Christian liberty when brethren of differing conscience live together. He establishes that love, not bare knowledge, must govern behaviour.

---

## v. 1 — “Now about food sacrificed to idols: We know that we all have knowledge. Knowledge puffs up, but love builds up.”

**TRADITIONAL READING**

- The phrase “now concerning” marks another question from the Corinthians’ letter (cf. 7:1, 7:25, 12:1). Paul first takes a detour to discuss knowledge rather than food directly, because the “strong” party was basing its conduct on the slogan “we all have knowledge.” (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-corinthians-8/; https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-corinthians-8-commentary)

- “Knowledge puffs up” and “love builds up” describe opposite kinds of growth: one inflates like a bubble, the other builds like a building. Christian behaviour is founded on love, not on knowledge alone. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-corinthians-8/)

- Gill notes that the knowledge here is mere notional, speculative knowledge — knowledge destitute of charity. True, sanctified knowledge makes a person humble; bare intellectual knowledge inflates the ego. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/1-corinthians-8.html)

- Precept Austin stresses this is a “gray chapter” — a passage dealing with an issue not directly addressed by explicit Scripture, where Christians must balance freedom in Christ with responsibility in love. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-corinthians-8-commentary)

**BAPTIST (Piper / Desiring God)**

- John Piper says Paul is addressing “the intelligent but unloving” — people who technically have the right theology but whose hearts are wrong. Knowledge is essential but not sufficient. The problem is the attitude behind it. (https://www.desiringgod.org/labs/love-builds-up)

---

## v. 2 — “The one who thinks he knows something does not yet know as he ought to know.”

**TRADITIONAL READING**

- If anyone is conceited about his knowledge, he proves by that very pride that he does not know as he ought. True knowledge would include knowing that one must consult the peace, comfort, and edification of his brother. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/1-corinthians-8.html)

- Ellicott adds that there must be a moral as well as intellectual element in knowledge if it is to be true knowledge. Without love to guide its use, it does not fulfil the true end of knowledge. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-corinthians-8.html — excerpt from search)

- The grammar uses a first-class conditional (“if anyone supposes…”), reflecting the settled arrogance of some Corinthians. (https://bible.org/seriespage/1-corinthians-8)

---

## v. 3 — “But the one who loves God is known by God.”

**TRADITIONAL READING**

- Paul’s emphasis is on love, not knowledge. The one who loves God — and therefore loves his brother — is the one “known” by God. This knowledge of God toward the believer is far more important than the believer’s own knowledge. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-corinthians-8/; https://bible.org/seriespage/1-corinthians-8)

- Gill says this person “is taught by him, made to know more by him… he is highly approved of, esteemed, and beloved by God.” (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/1-corinthians-8.html)

- Ellicott sees an “under-thought” here: the identity between knowing God and being known of Him. “Like water rising to its own level, the love and the knowledge rise as high as their source.” (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-corinthians-8.html — excerpt)

**BAPTIST (Piper)**

- Piper: the passage addresses those who have their facts right but hearts wrong. Loving God and being known by Him is the antidote to prideful knowledge. (https://www.desiringgod.org/labs/love-builds-up)

---

## v. 4 — “So about eating food sacrificed to idols: We know that an idol is nothing at all in the world, and that there is no God but one.”

**TRADITIONAL READING**

- Paul agrees with the theological premise of the “strong”: an idol has no real existence as a god. It is “nothing in the world” — not a competing deity. Because there is only one true God, idols are merely so-called gods. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-corinthians-8/)

- Gill notes Paul is speaking the language of the Jewish doctors, who said of idols, “there is nothing in an idol.” The Hebrew word for idols (*elilim*) means “things of nought.” (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/1-corinthians-8.html)

- Dr. Constable (from search excerpt): “Paul develops an airtight case based on a solid theological foundation (1 Corinthians 8:6). But then comes the ‘however’ (v. 7), and the argument moves in an entirely different direction.” (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/1-corinthians-8.html — excerpt)

- Bible.org notes this is the theological affirmation of monotheism. For those in the Judeo-Christian tradition there is only one creator/redeemer God. (https://bible.org/seriespage/1-corinthians-8)

---

## v. 5 — “For even if there are so-called gods, whether in heaven or on earth (as there are many so-called gods and lords)…”

**TRADITIONAL READING**

- Paul concedes there are many “so-called gods” — beings called gods by name but not by nature: angels, magistrates, sun, moon, stars, and the countless deities of the pagan pantheons. They are called gods but are not truly divine. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/1-corinthians-8.html)

- Enduring Word notes this refers to the “so-called gods” — “in the ancient world, there were many, many different gods — and even gods known as ‘the unknown god’ to cover any gods one might have missed (Acts 17:23).” (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-corinthians-8/)

---

## v. 6 — “yet for us there is but one God, the Father, from whom all things came and for whom we exist. And there is but one Lord, Jesus Christ, through whom all things came and through whom we exist.”

**TRADITIONAL READING**

- This is framed as the common confession of Christians over against pagan polytheism. Paul is not distinguishing Jesus from God as though Jesus were not divine. The Greek word *kurios* (“Lord”) was used in the Septuagint to render the divine name YHWH. Calling Jesus “Lord” is equivalent to calling Him deity. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-corinthians-8/)

- Gill explains that “one God, the Father” does not exclude the Son and Spirit from deity. If the Son were excluded from being “one God” by this clause, then by the same logic the Father would be excluded from being “one Lord” in the next clause — which is impossible. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/1-corinthians-8.html)

- “Through whom are all things” is language that can only be used of God the Creator. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-corinthians-8/)

- Precept Austin: Paul’s use of *kurios* “would have been recognized by Bible-reading people as a term equivalent to deity.” (https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-corinthians-8-commentary)

---

## v. 7 — “But not everyone has this knowledge. Some people are still so accustomed to idols that they eat such food as if it were sacrificed to an idol. And since their conscience is weak, it is defiled.”

**TRADITIONAL READING**

- Paul pivots: not every Christian in Corinth has fully internalised the truth that idols are nothing. Some, “with consciousness of the idol,” still regard the meat as genuinely tainted by its association with the false god. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-corinthians-8/)

- A “weak” conscience is not one that fails to function; it is one that is *wrongly informed*. It overworks — it binds where God has not bound. When such a person eats against his own conscience, even doing what is objectively permissible, his conscience is defiled because he acts without faith. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-corinthians-8/; https://bible.org/seriespage/1-corinthians-8)

- Gill: these weak believers “really thought in their own consciences, that there were something in an idol, they could not well tell what, that defiled meats offered to it.” They ate only through the pressure of others’ example, “not without some regret, and uneasiness of mind.” (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/1-corinthians-8.html)

**REFORMED (Ligonier)**

- Ligonier defines the weak conscience as one “influenced by sin and weakened by wrong information.” The problem is not an overly-scrupulous conscience per se (which may be prudent), but a conscience that wrongly binds where Scripture does not. The strong wrongly flaunted their freedom before the weak. (https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/weak-conscience)

---

## v. 8 — “But food does not bring us closer to God: We are no worse if we do not eat, and no better if we do.”

**TRADITIONAL READING**

- Eating or abstaining from meat is spiritually neutral. It neither commends us to God nor distances us from Him. “It is the clean heart, and not clean food, that will matter; and the weak brother confounds the two” (Robertson and Plummer, cited by Constable). (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/1-corinthians-8.html — excerpt)

- Gill: “meat commendeth us not to God… does not bring near, or give access to God.” Whether one eats or not, he is neither better nor worse in his standing before God. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/1-corinthians-8.html)

- Enduring Word applies this to modern debates: this is where most stumble on issues of Christian liberty (movies, drinking, music, television). They assume one stance or the other proves greater or lesser spirituality. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-corinthians-8/)

---

## v. 9 — “Be careful, however, that your freedom does not become a stumbling block to the weak.”

**TRADITIONAL READING**

- Because the matter is indifferent, “you must look elsewhere for your guide as to how you ought to act.” In things indifferent, the test is the effect on others. Liberty can become a stumbling-block — the cause of a brother taking a false step. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-corinthians-8.html — excerpt from search)

- “A stumbling block is any barrier to another individual’s personal relationship with God.” The strong Corinthians who returned to pagan temple feasts were disregarding how their participation affected brethren who still viewed it as worship or approval of the idol. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/1-corinthians-8.html — excerpt)

- The Expositor’s Bible: “Paul’s law, then, is that liberty must be tempered by love; that the individual must consider the society of which he forms a part.” (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/teb/1-corinthians-8.html — excerpt)

---

## v. 10 — “For if someone with a weak conscience sees you who are well informed eating in an idol’s temple, will he not be encouraged to eat food sacrificed to idols?”

**TRADITIONAL READING**

- The verb translated “encouraged” (or “emboldened”) is actually the Greek word for “built up” (*oikodomeō*) — the very word used positively in v. 1 for what love does. Paul uses it sarcastically: the strong are “building up” the weak brother — into sin. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-corinthians-8/; https://bible.org/seriespage/1-corinthians-8)

- The situation is not just buying meat at the market but dining *in the idol’s temple itself*, participating in the full cultic meal (Gordon Fee, cited by Bible.org, thinks this refers to actually attending the temple feast, which sometimes involved sexual activity). (https://bible.org/seriespage/1-corinthians-8)

- Gill: the weak brother, seeing the knowledgeable brother eating in the temple, is “emboldened… with boldness, and without fear, to eat those things which are offered to idols, contrary to his light, and knowledge, and conscience.” (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/1-corinthians-8.html)

---

## v. 11 — “So this weak brother, for whom Christ died, is destroyed by your knowledge.”

**TRADITIONAL READING**

- “Destroyed” (*apollumi*) is strong language. Paul “evidently anticipated the weaker brother returning to idolatry, the next step after participating in a feast in an idol temple.” The strong brother dare not view the weak brother’s scruples as insignificant — Christ died for him. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/1-corinthians-8.html — excerpt)

- Every word in this verse aggravates the sin: it is a “brother,” a “weak” brother, ruined “through your knowledge,” and he is one “for whom Christ died.” (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/1-corinthians-8.html)

- Bible.org: “This is a sarcastic comment… The Corinthian church was proud of their knowledge. Here Paul shows knowledge can be a disaster.” (https://bible.org/seriespage/1-corinthians-8)

- Gill addresses a theological concern: the phrase “for whom Christ died” is put interrogatively (“shall the weak brother perish, for whom Christ died?”) and does not of itself prove universal redemption. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/1-corinthians-8.html)

**BAPTIST (Piper)**

- Piper: “With your knowledge, you are hurting your brother for whom Christ died. Wow.” The unloving use of knowledge against a fellow Christian amounts to sin against Jesus Himself. (https://www.desiringgod.org/labs/love-builds-up)

---

## v. 12 — “By sinning against your brothers in this way and wounding their weak conscience, you sin against Christ.”

**TRADITIONAL READING**

- To wound a weak brother’s conscience is not merely to offend a fellow Christian — it is to sin against Christ Himself. The Corinthians who abused their liberty “might have thought it was a small matter to offend their weak brothers, but they did not understand they offended Jesus Christ.” (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-corinthians-8/)

- This is the very opposite of the great commandments to love God and neighbour (Matt. 22:37–39). (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/1-corinthians-8.html — excerpt)

---

## v. 13 — “Therefore, if what I eat causes my brother to stumble, I will never eat meat again, so that I will not cause him to stumble.”

**TRADITIONAL READING**

- Paul states his own solemn resolution: he would rather never eat meat again than cause a brother to stumble. The Greek has a very strong triple negative construction (“I will never, no never eat meat”). Freedom in Christ should edify, not destroy. (https://bible.org/seriespage/1-corinthians-8; https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-corinthians-8/)

- This does not imply Paul became a vegetarian; it means he will never eat meat sacrificed to an idol, or eat in an idol’s temple, if that would harm a brother. (https://bible.org/seriespage/1-corinthians-8)

- Ellicott: “If a matter of food cause a brother to fall in his Christian course, I will certainly never again eat any kind of flesh, lest I should be the cause of so making him to fall.” (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-corinthians-8.html — excerpt)

- Enduring Word adds an important qualifier: “Paul would never allow this principle to be a way for a legalist to make demands and bind a Christian walking in liberty.” Paul distinguishes between a genuinely weak brother who might be tempted to sin, and a legalist whose sensibilities are merely offended. We protect the former; we do not appease the latter. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-corinthians-8/)

**BAPTIST (Piper)**

- Piper: “Paul loves his brothers and sisters in Christ so much that if he knew that their seeing him eat meat would cause them to stumble, then he simply will stop eating meat. He’ll go vegan. Eating meat is not that big of a deal compared to loving his brother.” (https://www.desiringgod.org/labs/love-builds-up)

---

## Distinctive Traditional Emphases

- **Reformed (Ligonier)**: The weak conscience is “awakened” but “weakened by wrong information.” Legalism arises when the weak dictate others’ consciences or call sinful what God has not forbidden. The strong must not flaunt freedom, and the weak must not become judgmental legalists. (https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/weak-conscience)

- **Baptist (Gill / Piper)**: Gill provides the most detailed verse-by-verse exposition from a Calvinistic Baptist perspective, emphasising the distinction between true, sanctified knowledge and mere notional knowledge. Piper stresses the “life of the mind” must be paired with a “love of man” — the heart must not lag behind the head. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/1-corinthians-8.html; https://www.desiringgod.org/labs/love-builds-up)

- **Pentecostal/Charismatic (Enduring Word / David Guzik)**: Guzik emphasises the Spirit-filled principle that love, not knowledge, is the goal. The point is practical and pastoral: being “right” is less important than loving well. The sermon applies the text to modern grey-area debates and warns against both legalism and license. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-corinthians-8/)

---
